summary: Arm's Platform Security Architecture (PSA) is a family of security specifications and reference implementations for devices. This informational RFC describes the attestation token that PSA-compliant devices can generate, which reports on the device's state and identity for verification by a remote party.

eli5.summary: A device can hand over a signed report saying "this is who I am and how I'm set up." This describes the form of such a report for devices made following Arm's design.

subtitle: The exact claims and encoding that an Arm PSA device uses to prove its identity and software state to a remote verifier.

tldr.problem: Attestation tokens from PSA-compliant devices are consumed by services outside the device, so the syntax, meaning, encoding and protection of the claims must be pinned down for interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The PSA attestation token is a profile of the Entity Attestation Token (EAT). Its claims are encoded in CBOR and wrapped in a signed COSE_Sign1 or MAC-protected COSE_Mac0 structure produced by the PSA Root of Trust.
tldr.outcome: This is an Informational Independent Submission documenting a vendor extension to the RATS architecture. It is not a standard and not an IETF product.

today: RFC 9783 is an Informational Independent Submission that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is not a standard and not an IETF product, and the RFC Editor makes no statement about its value for implementation or deployment.

sections.title: What the PSA Attestation Token Is
sections.content:
Arm's Platform Security Architecture (PSA) is a set of hardware and firmware security specifications with reference implementations and a certification program. Devices that comply can produce attestation tokens, which this document specifies.

In the terms of RFC 9334, the token is Evidence produced by the output of PSA's Initial Attestation API. As a design decision it is a profile of the Entity Attestation Token (EAT). Because the tokens are consumed by services outside the device, the RFC describes the exact syntax and semantics of the claims and how they are encoded and cryptographically protected.

The document is an Independent Submission. It says plainly that it documents a vendor extension to the RATS architecture and is not a standard.
sections.eli5: It is the rule book for one maker's signed ID-and-health card for devices, written so other people can read the cards correctly.

sections.title: The PSA Attester Model
sections.content:
The PSA Attester has exactly one Attesting Environment and one or more Target Environments. The Attesting Environment has two parts. At boot, the Main Bootloader measures the Target Environments and stores the results in secure memory called Main Boot State. At run time, the Initial Attestation Service, running in the Secure Processing Environment (SPE), answers requests from the Non-Secure Processing Environment (NSPE) through the PSA attestation API. It collects claims from Main Boot State and signs them with the Initial Attestation Key (IAK) to produce Evidence.

"Initial" refers to the first foundational stages that establish the chain of trust. Measuring Target Environments after that is outside the specification. The Target Environments can be of four types: PSA Root of Trust (RoT) parameters, the updateable PSA RoT, an optional Application RoT, and the loader of the application software running in the NSPE.
sections.eli5: When the device wakes up, a helper writes down what it loaded in a safe place. Later, a second helper reads that note, signs it with a secret pen, and hands it to the checker.

sections.title: The PSA Claims
sections.content:
Claims are defined in CDDL and grouped by purpose. The nonce (EAT claim key 10) carries the verifier's challenge, MUST be 32, 48 or 64 bytes, and MUST be present. The Client ID (key 2394) is a signed integer naming the caller's security domain: negative for the NSPE, positive for the SPE, and 0 is not permitted.

For identification, the Instance ID (EAT ueid, key 256) is 33 bytes: a first byte of 0x01 followed by the 32-byte unique identifier of the IAK. The Implementation ID (32 bytes) identifies the hardware assembly of the immutable PSA RoT, not a particular instance. The optional Certification Reference is a string of thirteen digits, a dash and five digits.

The Security Lifecycle claim (key 2395) carries the major state in bits 15:8 and an implementation-defined minor state in bits 7:0. A Verifier can only trust reports from the PSA RoT in the SECURED or NON_PSA_ROT_DEBUG major states. The optional Boot Seed (key 268) is 8 to 32 bytes and distinguishes boot sessions.

The Software Components claim lists the code and configuration loaded by the PSA RoT. Each entry MUST carry a measurement value (a hash of 256 bits or stronger), and the signer ID MUST be present to comply with the PSA security model. Optional attributes are a measurement type such as BL, PRoT, ARoT, App or TS, a version, and a description naming the hash algorithm.

Two claims help receivers: the optional Verification Service Indicator, a hint for locating a verification service that a Relying Party may ignore, and the Profile Definition, which MUST be present.
sections.eli5: The form has boxes for a secret word from the checker, who is asking, which device and model this is, what stage of life it is in, and a list of the software it loaded.

sections.title: Profiles, Encoding and Signing
sections.content:
The RFC defines a Baseline profile with common requirements and a TFM profile that builds on it. The TFM profile fits the code base of the TF-M reference implementation, and its profile identifier is tag:psacertified.org,2023:psa#tfm.

Tokens are encoded as CBOR with definite-length strings, arrays and maps. The Attester may not emit preferred serialization, so the Verifier MUST be a variation-tolerant CBOR decoder. Protection comes from wrapping the claims in a CBOR Web Token (RFC 8392): a tagged (18) COSE_Sign1 for asymmetric keys, or a tagged (17) COSE_Mac0 for symmetric keys. The CWT tag (61) is not used, and the claims are never sent as a detached EAT bundle.

The TFM profile requires receivers to accept ES256, ES384 and ES512 with COSE_Sign1 and HMAC256/256, HMAC384/384 and HMAC512/512 with COSE_Mac0, and requires senders to use one of them. Freshness uses the nonce claim, which can also carry an epoch handle of 8 to 64 octets. An earlier profile, PSA_IOT_PROFILE_1, used private-use claim keys that are now deprecated, and Verifiers are RECOMMENDED to accept both old and new tokens while devices upgrade.
sections.eli5: The form is written in a compact code and sealed with a signature, so if anyone changes a word the seal breaks. Checkers are told to be flexible about how the code is written down.

sections.title: Verification, Security and Privacy
sections.content:
A Verifier checks encoding and signature first. For a raw public key, the Instance ID helps locate the verification key. For a certified key, X.509 path validation up to a trusted CA, including revocation checking, MUST succeed. Certificates can be inlined with the x5chain COSE header parameter at the cost of a larger token. Verifiers typically compare claims such as Implementation ID, the software measurement values and signer IDs, and the Certification Reference with registered reference values.

On security, MAC authentication is NOT RECOMMENDED because of key management costs and protocol complexity. A PSA Attester MUST NOT provide Evidence to an untrusted challenger. On privacy, tokens may contain information unique to a device and so could single it out for tracking. Deployments with privacy needs must take care that the token is only used to provision anonymous or pseudonym keys.
sections.eli5: The checker first makes sure the seal is real and from the right maker, then compares the form with a list of what is allowed. Because each form can identify one gadget, privacy-minded users need to be careful who sees it.
